claims.text: The as-synthesized near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles form a single-phase solid solution.
Near-equiatomic composition gives the nanoparticles high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy kinetically suppresses atomic diffusion.
Suppressed atomic diffusion inhibits phase segregation.
Suppressed atomic diffusion inhibits nanoparticle coarsening.
Inhibiting diffusion, segregation, and coarsening preserves nanoparticle structure and chemical stability at high service temperatures.
Moving composition away from equiatomic ratios reduces configurational-entropy stabilization.
High configurational entropy increases the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement and diffusion.
Reduced entropy stabilization makes off-equiatomic nanoparticles more susceptible to structural transformation.
Reduced entropy stabilization makes off-equiatomic nanoparticles more susceptible to grain coarsening.
Reduced entropy stabilization makes off-equiatomic nanoparticles more susceptible to elemental segregation.
After identical high-temperature exposure, equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation, grain growth, and surface elemental segregation than off-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Greater structural degradation in off-equiatomic nanoparticles will cause a larger decline in catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The proposed entropy-mediated stability mechanism applies over 473–1923 K in controlled service-relevant atmospheres.
Strongly oxidizing environments or other rapid chemical processes can override configurational-entropy stabilization.
Particle size and synthesis-induced defects may also contribute to stability.
